title: The Teacher as a Mensch
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart uses Bruna Martinuzzi's The Leader as a Mensch to name something he has circled for years: the inner work of teaching. He is explicit that this is an aspirational read rather than a practical one, a book he returns to when he needs a reminder of where he would like to head, and he reproduces Martinuzzi's definition in full because the word was new to him. That definition does the heavy lifting, describing a person in whose presence we feel safe, who makes us feel good about ourselves, who earns respect without demanding it and often leads from the side by force of example, whether in the boardroom, classroom or living room. Stuart then borrows Seth Godin's framing of a career as a series of projects rather than jobs, and reads his own reading and writing life that way: a Common Core project, then the project that became These 6 Things. The next project is only half-formed, and he is content to leave it so, but he names the question it circles, how do we become the kinds of teachers from whom great teaching tends to flow. His observation is that such teachers exist in every school he visits, differ widely in style, and share a place of inner strength and clarity that gives their classrooms outsized effect.
points: The piece names a category most craft writing skips, the inner work of teaching, and offers Mensch as a usable model for it.

Martinuzzi's definition supplies observable markers rather than virtues in the abstract: earning respect without demanding it, leading from the side by example, being someone in whose presence people feel safe.
Godin's career-as-projects framing is used practically, letting Stuart read his own reading and writing life as a sequence of questions rather than a sequence of posts.
The governing question is worth keeping: how do we become the kinds of teachers from whom great teaching tends to flow, which shifts attention from technique to the person.
The supporting observation is that such teachers exist in every school and differ widely in style, which rules out a single method and points instead to inner strength and clarity.
quotes: Every time I pick up Bruna Martinuzzi's little book, The Leader as a Mensch, I'm given a mark that's well out in front of me.
In a special way, it is an aspirational read — I pick it up when I need a reminder of where I'd like to head.
It describes an individual who is higher on the evolutionary scale, a person in whose presence we feel safe; a person who makes us feel good about ourselves.
There are no organizational assessments for Mensch-hood. You know when you are in the presence of a Mensch.
Blogger emeritus Seth Godin has this way of looking at one's career not as a series of jobs but as a series of projects.

Their styles differ, they've got different strengths and weaknesses, but they teach from this place of inner strength and clarity, and as a result, their classrooms have an outsized impact on the long-term flourishing outcomes of kids.
